extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology and literary criticism (graduate-level readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic framework for evaluating narrative voice: the narrator's diegetic level, relationship to the story, grammatical person, functions, and the narratee; focused on diagnosing types (heterodiegetic/homodiegetic/autodiegetic), shifts, and the ideological/communicative roles of narrators (with Proust as a central case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person (first/third) — grammatical vs narratorial distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat 'first-person' vs 'third-person' as simply grammatical choices; these locutions are inadequate because they conflate two different situations: the narrator's self-designation and the identity of narrator with a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether first-person verbs indicate (a) the narrator's utterance as such (e.g., Virgil's 'I sing...') or (b) identity between narrator and a character (e.g., Crusoe's 'I was born...'). The novelist's choice is between two narrative postures (having a character tell the story vs having an external narrator), not merely between grammatical forms. Beware of assuming that grammatical person maps directly to narratorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterodiegetic vs Homodiegetic status of the narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize narrators by whether they are inside the story they narrate (homodiegetic) or outside it (heterodiegetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to classify: Homer and Flaubert are heterodiegetic (absent from the narrative), Gil Blas and the narrator of Wuthering Heights are homodiegetic (present as characters). This distinction is fundamental to narrative analysis and affects how authority, knowledge, and involvement are read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autodiegetic and degrees of presence within homodiegetic narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Within homodiegetic narrators distinguish those who are the hero of their story (autodiegetic) from those who play secondary/observer roles; presence is not binary but has degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve 'autodiegetic' for narrators who are the hero (e.g., Gil Blas). Recognize intermediate cases (Lockwood, Watson, Marlow, Ishmael) where the narrator is present but not the protagonist. Absence is absolute, but presence varies — narrative analysis must register these degrees because they affect focalization and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diegetic level matrix (extradiegetic vs intradiegetic × homo/heterodiegetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent narrator's status by two coordinates: narrative level (extradiegetic/intradiegetic) and relationship to the story (heterodiegetic/homodiegetic), yielding four paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four basic types as analytic paradigms with canonical examples: (1) extradiegetic-heterodiegetic (Homer), (2) extradiegetic-homodiegetic (Gil Blas), (3) intradiegetic-heterodiegetic (Scheherazade), (4) intradiegetic-homodiegetic (Ulysses in Books IX–XII). This matrix clarifies layered narrating instances and helps detect reversals or condensations of instances in complex texts (e.g., Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronominal shifts and 'pronominal vertigo' as norm infraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in grammatical person used to designate the same character (e.g., suddenly moving from 'I' to 'he' or vice versa) are to be read as violations of an implicit narratorial norm, or as deliberate modernist effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sudden shifts (Balzac's Autre etude de femme, Jean Santeuil) as signs of narrative pathology in classical novels or as deliberate experimentation in modern literature (Borges). Note such shifts as symptomatic of changes in the relation between narrator and character and as cues to narrative instability or complex identity play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metadiegetic narration and the performative power of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize metadiegetic narratives (narratives within narratives) and their potential to function performatively — to give life, take life, or 'trap' events into happening (e.g., an oracle told in a future tense that sets events in motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse instances like the oracle in Oedipus (a metadiegetic future-tense narrative that 'throws into gear' the events it describes) or Scheherazade (narrative that gives life). Consider how stories told within a story can operate causally or instrumentally within the diegesis (Proust: 'love told' as instrument of Destiny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of the narrator (narrative, directing, communicative, attestation, ideological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which of several possible functions the narrator emphasizes: (1) the strictly narrative function (telling the story), (2) directing function (metanarrative staging/organizing), (3) communication/phatic-conative function (orientation to narratee/reader), (4) emotive/testimonial function (attestation of source and memory), and (5) ideological function (authorized commentary and didactic discourse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Jakobson-style functional distinctions to analyse narrative passages. For directing function, look for 'stage directions' or advance notices and recalls. For communicative function, look for explicit addresses to the narratee or reader. For attestation, note memory-claims and indications of source or precision. For ideological function, note authorized commentary or didactic pronouncements — some narrators (e.g., Proust's Marcel) concentrate this function more than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's monopoly or distribution of the ideological function
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether ideological/commentary functions are monopolized by the narrator or distributed among characters; this affects the narrative's relation to authorial voice and realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Proust the narrator (Marcel) retains quasi-monopoly of ideological commentary; by contrast, authors like Dostoevsky or Mann transfer commentary to characters, creating dialogic or polyphonic speculation. Note whether characters serve as 'organs of truth' (authorial proxies) or remain objects of observation whose errors illuminate the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratee as diegetic interlocutor distinct from (implied) reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the narratee as an element of the narrating situation located at the same diegetic level as the narrator and not simply conflated with the real reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether the narratee is present, absent, implied, or fictional, and how the narrator orients discourse toward that narratee (e.g., epistolary monodies where the absent receiver dominates). Do not assume narratee = reader; trace diegetic placement and its effects on address and communicative function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and eventual convergence of narrating I and narrated I (hero/narrator gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: In autobiographical-form narratives, distinguish the narrating I (erzählendes Ich) and the narrated I (erzähletes Ich): they typically differ in age/knowledge and may converge through revelation, altering voice and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Proust's Recherche as paradigm: the narrating I can treat the narrated I condescendingly until a decisive revelation causes blending of voices (hero's past experience and narrator's understanding coincide). Watch for changes in tense, proliferation of indirect discourse, and shifts from imperfect to present-tense authoritative formulations ('I understood', 'I knew').

rubrics_metrics.name: Omniscience vs autodiegetic first-person and coherence tensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate tensions when a first-person/autodiegetic narrator displays omniscient knowledge beyond the hero's possible experience; this can produce plural focalization or perceived incoherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proustian narrating often combines first-person autodiegetic voice with occasional omniscient commentary. Note the narrative problems this causes (e.g., knowledge of other characters' inner states that exceeds the hero's access) and how the text justifies or conceals such overreach (stratification of instances, prior metanarrative framing, or deliberate mixing of voices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative organization devices: advance notices, recalls, indications of source
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify 'directing indications' or metanarrative signals that organize the text (advance notices, recalls, attributions of source, stage directions) and consider their rhetorical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit organizational remarks (as in Cooper or Mann examples) and for authorial remarks about the limits or sources of knowledge. These devices shape reader expectation, manage temporal flow, and mark the narrator's directing function; their verbosity or intrusiveness is a stylistic and evaluative criterion.
